Rule and evidence

What UPSC 2027 is most likely to draw on

Zola tracks the events of the last eighteen months, scores each one on evidence you can see, and ranks what deserves your hours. It cannot predict questions. UPSC writes each paper fresh. It can tell you which textbook hooks the news has made live.

Zola ranks topics, never questions. Every score shows its evidence and every claim names its source.

What changed from v1

This edition rebuilds the model on a research round that coded every GS-I and CSAT question from 2021 to 2026 against the official papers and keys, and tested the old rules on the actual papers.

  • Six signals replace four. v1 scored size, static hook, setter fit and recency window. The new signals are static hook, settled stage, persistence across official milestones, echo in past papers, firsts and changes, and scale. Each has a definition, and each event shows its scores.
  • Recency is off. In 2022-2026 the news behind questions was spread evenly across eighteen months. Window now decides eligibility, not priority, and items 18 to 36 months old stay as a discounted background tier.
  • Tiers are ranked, not thresholded. v1 put 16 of 32 events in Tier S and called them near-certain. Tier S is now the top 15% and is a study order, not a probability.
  • The forecast ranges are honest about error. The "mean reversion" rule in v1 was tested on 2023-2026 and barely beat repeating last year. The ranges are now ±5 questions, and the Model lab shows why.
  • 57 events with stable ids and explicit source status. 25 additions came from official releases, and several v1 facts were confirmed or corrected; the corrections are listed below.

What to remember in six weeks. UPSC turns small, bounded facts hanging off a recent story into static questions. Learn the hook, not the headline.

Mains angle. Every event's static hook is a ready Mains point: the Article, Act or treaty clause gives an answer its spine, and the news gives it a current example.

Check yourself

1. Why is recency no longer a scoring signal?

Because the hooks behind 2022-2026 questions were spread evenly across the eighteen months before each exam (24, 24 and 26 hooks in the 0-6, 6-12 and 12-18 month bands). An event from last year was as likely to be used as one from last month.

2. What does Tier S mean in this edition?

The top 15% of events by score under the current weights. It is a study order, not a probability that a question will be asked.

3. Why does a tracker built only on PIB fall short?

PIB supplied about 36% of the dated hooks behind 2021-2026 questions. UN bodies, foreign governments, award committees and science agencies supplied the rest, so they need their own feeds.

    The evidence behind the model

    Everything here comes from Zola's own coding of the official UPSC papers and keys for 2021 to 2026: 600 GS-I questions and 480 CSAT questions, each labelled under one rule. Coaching-site tallies disagree with each other by two to five questions per subject, which is why this edition codes from the papers itself.

    How the paper has been changing, 2021 to 2026

    The same numbers as a table

    What holds up from v1's pattern notes: 2026 had 21 history and culture questions, 16 of them ancient history and art, and none from medieval history. It had 8 negatively worded stems and one dropped question. 2023 had 47 "how many of the above" questions, which is why elimination stopped working that year. Questions linked to recent news rose to 20 in 2025 and 22 in 2026, up from 10 to 13 in earlier years.

    "Format" uses one fixed precedence rule across all six years; "news link" counts questions whose premise rests on a dated event within 18 months of the exam (Y), static questions with a recent hook (partial), and the rest.

    Why coaching tallies of the same paper disagree

    Zola's subject counts were compared cell by cell with three published analyses of the same papers. Each disagreement is a different coding choice, not a mistake on either side, but it means a single "subject count" is never as exact as it looks.

    How old was the news UPSC used?

    Each bar counts the questions whose news hook was that many months old on exam day, across 88 current-affairs-linked questions from 2021 to 2026. Move the slider to choose how far back your tracker looks.

    The spread is close to even, which is why recency is off in the scoring. A separate check of 35 questions coded as having no hook found 6 with a hook 18 to 36 months old, so this edition keeps those older items as a discounted background tier.

    Where the hooks came from

    The issuing body behind each question's dated trigger, 2021 to 2026. PIB is the largest single feed and still under two fifths of the total.

    Did the old scoring find the questions? A backtest

    To test a weighted-signal approach like v1's, a pool of candidate events was built using only information available before each exam, scored on the old signals, frozen, and only then compared with the paper.

    ExamCandidatesMain sourceHits in top 100What it showed
    2026164PIB, 110 of 1640For 8 of 10 sampled misses, the source sat inside the feeds the pool claimed to cover; the pool simply did not collect it.
    2025169PIB, 161 of 1691One hit, the revised Rashtriya Gokul Mission (Q30), ranked 43rd.

    Two of the test's seven signals (persistence and past-paper echo) never fired on any of the 333 candidates, and the static-hook signal scored the maximum on 79% of them, so it could not separate anything. The lessons built into this edition: collect widely before ranking, grade the hook instead of ticking it, and do not claim the weights are validated. They are hypotheses you can adjust.

    This was a retrospective test, not a blind one: the papers had already been seen.

    Does a low subject bounce back? Testing mean reversion

    v1 called mean reversion the main statistical signal for subject counts. Forecasting each of 2023-2026 from earlier years only, across eight subject groups:

    RuleAverage miss (questions per subject)
    Half last year, half the long-run average3.0
    Same as last year3.1
    Long-run average3.2
    Average of the last three years3.4

    The correlation between how far a subject sat from its average and how much it moved the next year was −0.22 across 40 cases: a weak pull back, not a law. The 2027 ranges in the Model lab use the best rule, with a ±5 band that covered 80% of past misses.

    How often do concepts come back?

    Two ceilings, both upper bounds rather than measurements. A published analysis of 1,299 questions from 2013-2025 claimed half the paper recurs; its own numbers allow at most 34% of questions to repeat a concept asked in an earlier year. A first pass of the 2025 paper against 2024 found 2 exact and 10 close concept-repeat pairs, and 32 pairs that matched only at topic level. Repeats are real but modest. Topic overlap is common; true repeats are not.

    The full recurrence study is incomplete, so the "echo in past papers" signal uses only matches found in Zola's 2021-2026 coding. Where none was found, the event is scored neutral, not zero.

    The exam machinery

    General category Prelims cut-off

    Official UPSC cut-off records. The 2023 low matches the hardest year by format.

    What one attempt is worth

    GS-I: +2, −0.67 for a wrong answer. CSAT: +2.5, −0.83. Blank scores zero. Attempting pays above 25% accuracy. For the CSAT gate itself, open category C.

    The CSAT gate in numbers

    Zola's recode of all 480 CSAT questions (numeracy includes data sufficiency). Solve times are coded estimates. The paper always holds more than 120 minutes of work, but the 27 quickest questions, enough for 66 marks with no errors, take about half an hour. The gate is lost on accuracy, not speed. Practise it in category C.

    How to read a coaching "hit rate"

    ClaimWhat it actually measures
    EdMe: 62.6% average recall, 2020-2025 back-testSelf-reported share of tested topic labels matched by its lists. Recall, not precision, and not independently audited.
    EdMe: 63 of 74 current-affairs questions in 2026 (85%)Recall on questions it classified as current-affairs-linked itself, from a module published the day before the exam.
    IASbaba: 73% hit ratio, 202556 direct and 15 indirect matches to its classes and materials, mapped after the exam.
    Insights IAS: 35+ direct hits, CSAT 2026Questions mapped to its CSAT classes after the exam; no denominator shown.
    OptimizeIAS: 40+ questions predicted each year, 2022-2025Topics, themes and patterns counted together; no frozen list or denominator.

    A long list always "covers" many questions. Without a list frozen before the exam, a denominator and a count of misses, a hit rate measures how much was taught, not how well anything was predicted. Zola's own backtest is reported above with its misses.

    Past papers, coded

    All 600 GS-I and 480 CSAT questions from 2021 to 2026, each coded by subject, format, news link and official answer. Question text is not reproduced: each entry carries a concept label so you can find a topic, then read the question in the official paper.

    GS-I answers are from UPSC's final keys, and the 2026 provisional key. "Dropped" means UPSC removed the question from scoring. 2021 entries carry few concept labels; use the syllabus area and news hook. 2022 question numbers follow a different booklet from Series A. CSAT solve times and difficulty are coded estimates, not timed trials.

    Sources and limits

    Official documents behind the numbers

    • UPSC GS Paper I and GS Paper II question papers and keys, 2018-2026, Series A (2026: provisional key, the first UPSC has published). Retrieved from upsc.gov.in or archived copies of its pages, with file hashes. The 2025 GS-I final key was read but its file could not be archived.
    • UPSC Annual Calendar 2027 (as on 20 May 2026): notification 13 Jan, applications to 2 Feb, Prelims 23 May 2027. Calendar PDF
    • UPSC CSE 2026 notice: marking scheme and the 33% CSAT qualifying rule. Notice PDF
    • UPSC cut-off records, 2020-2025. Previous papers archive
    • PIB releases cited on each event; Census 2027 backgrounder. Census PDF
    • UNFCCC (COP31), CBD (COP17), IMF (Annual Meetings), WTO, UN Treaty Collection, UNESCO, Ramsar, WIPO, UNDP and the G20 for international events.

    How the research was done

    Two research rounds in September and October 2026. The first gathered official facts, the forward calendar and claims made by coaching institutes. The second coded every 2021-2026 question, measured how old the news behind each question was, backtested the v1 scoring on the 2025 and 2026 papers, and recoded every CSAT question against the official keys. Each finding was tagged as official, data, expert opinion or speculation.

    What this edition does not claim

    • No probabilities. Scores rank study priority; they are not chances that a question appears.
    • No validated weights. The default weights are reasoned hypotheses. The only backtest available argued against the old ones, not for the new ones.
    • No exact subject counts. Bands are ±5 questions because that is how much the paper has actually moved.
    • No complete recurrence study. The past-paper echo signal uses 2021-2026 matches only.

    Known gaps

    • Events marked "From v1" were not re-checked in the October round. Check them before relying on a detail. Two are flagged "Needs checking".
    • Which textbook a question came from could be verified for only a handful of the 600 questions.
    • Past-paper references use the question numbers from Zola's coding. For 2022 those follow a different booklet from Series A, so check the topic, not just the number.
    • No official data exists on how many candidates clear the CSAT gate.

    Category B (Hacking the System) and category C (CSAT Question Forge) keep their own source notes at the end of each file. In this edition every one of the Forge's 68 past-paper answers was rechecked against the official UPSC keys for 2023-2026, and all 68 matched.
